\label{ch:aquel}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can point at something away from us both.}

I can point at something away from us both.

\section[aquel]{aquel — the far one, and an old friend in disguise}

\label{lesson:ES-C59-aquel}



\begin{quote}
Mine, here: \emph{este libro}. Yours, there: \emph{ese libro}.

Now the one across the room, belonging to neither of us.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{aquel libro} — \emph{that book over there}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\emph{\textbf{aquel}} \emph{libro} & that book, over there \\
\emph{\textbf{aquella}} \emph{casa} & that house, over there \\
\emph{\textbf{aquellos}} \emph{libros} & those books, over there \\
\emph{\textbf{aquellas}} \emph{casas} & those houses, over there \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Look at the middle of that word. \emph{\textbf{-el-}}. You have met it before, in your \textbf{first chapter}.

Latin \emph{\textbf{ille}} went two ways at once. Said quickly and without stress, leaning on the noun after it, it wore down to \emph{\textbf{el}} — the article. Said with stress, and propped up in front with \textbf{accu-} (roughly \emph{look, there}), it stayed a pointing word: \textbf{accu + ille $\to$ aquel}.

So \emph{el} and \emph{aquel} are the same Latin word, and the difference between them is two thousand years of one being emphasised and the other not.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
That leaves Spanish with \textbf{three}, where English has two:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\emph{este} & by me \\
\emph{ese} & by you \\
\emph{aquel} & by neither of us \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English collapses the last two into \emph{that} and then patches the difference back on when it matters — \emph{that one over there}. Spanish keeps the three apart in the word itself, so it never needs the patch.

And the middle one is the one to watch. If you find yourself reaching for \emph{aquel} because the thing is a few steps away, stop and ask the real question: is it near the person you are talking to? If it is, it is \emph{ese}, however far it is from you.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{este libro}, \emph{ese libro}, \emph{aquel libro}
  \item \emph{aquella casa}, \emph{aquellos libros}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Three words, three places. Which one is by the person you are talking to? (\emph{\textbf{Ese}}.)

And what did \emph{el} and \emph{aquel} both start out as? (Latin \emph{\textbf{ille}} — one worn down, one propped up.)
\end{tcolorbox}
